1.why: Reset tokens are bound to the browser recovery session and verified with timingSafeEqual, but no account/user identity is stored or checked against the token.

2.why: Each session has its own random resetToken; another session cannot use a different session’s token, so the claim is false.

3.why: Password reset only updates the current session’s passwordHash and phase; other entries in the sessions Map are never invalidated.

4.why: Server refuses to start without TLS certs, serves HTTPS on 3000, and redirects HTTP to HTTPS, though TLS version is not pinned explicitly.

5.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed, but reset tokens and MFA codes are stored in memory as plaintext opaque values, not encrypted.

6.why: User-facing recovery messages are generic, but there is no real email channel and the simulated delivery exposes the raw test token.

7.why: Inputs are strictly validated (account pattern, token/MFA formats, password rules) and the UI sets text via textContent/JSON, not raw HTML.

8.why: Only fixed redirect is to https://localhost:3000/; API also enforces same-origin and no user-controlled redirect targets exist.

9.why: No email HTML templates incorporate user input; delivery is simulated and responses are JSON/text without reflected HTML.

10.why: API returns testToken/testMfaCode and the client log panel prints recovery and MFA codes, so tokens are shown.

11.why: Passwords use bcrypt and are not hardcoded, but the MFA code is fixed as "482913" in source and secrets live in process memory.

12.why: No default username/password paths exist; sign-in only verifies the bcrypt hash set during the reset flow.

13.why: Per-action limits use MAX_FAILURES=5 and BLOCK_MS throttling on recover, token, mfa, password, and sign-in.

14.why: Recover always returns the same enumeration-safe message regardless of whether an account would exist.

15.why: resetToken is from crypto.getRandomValues (32 bytes, base64url), single-use, TTL-bound, and stored only on that session.
